data.text/markdown:
The Coastline That Never Smooths

Paper: The boundary of neural network trainability is fractal (Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, 2024, arXiv 2402.06184) Pick two learning rates for a tiny neural network: one for the input layer, one for the output layer. Train it. Either the loss settles (trainable) or it blows up (divergent). Color one pixel by the outcome. Repeat for every pair on a grid and you get a map of trainability. Intuition says the border between the two regions should behave like a coastline on a school atlas: wiggly from afar, smooth once you zoom in. The paper's claim, and this notebook's centerpiece, is that it is a coastline in the mathematical sense: a true fractal. Zoom in ten times, a thousand times, and it never smooths. New bays, islands, and inlets of trainability keep appearing at every scale. Why that matters: this boundary is where every hyperparameter search lives. If it is fractal, there is no safe margin near the edge, and "just tune the learning rate a little" sits on geometry with structure at every scale. This notebook rebuilds the map from scratch, lets you sail it, and then asks the question the paper deliberately excluded: does the coastline survive the noise of real minibatch training? The answer is measured, not argued.
  1. Rebuilds the fractal from scratch. Every pixel is a real gradient descent training run, executed live on this notebook's GPU (a GPU-less fork drops to a smaller grid and still works).
  2. Lets you sail the coastline. Pick any box and the map recomputes at full resolution inside it.
  3. Measures what noise does to it. We track the boundary's fractal dimension as minibatch noise grows, and watch the coastline dissolve.
(The paper's alphaXiv page also carries an AI summary, audio overview, and a discussion tab if you want the short version first.)

data.text/markdown:
1. A map where every pixel is a training run

The setup mirrors the paper's reference implementation exactly:
  • a 1-hidden-layer tanh network, 16 units wide, in mean-field parameterization
  • a fixed random dataset of 272 points (as many data points as the network has parameters)
  • full-batch gradient descent for 500 steps
  • the two axes are the log learning rates of the input layer and the output layer
Each pixel gets a signed convergence score: negative (cool colors) means training settled, positive (warm colors) means it diverged, and the magnitude encodes how fast. The score, the network, and the color normalization follow the author's public reference code (MIT), reimplemented in PyTorch and validated against the author's own rendering.

Cool region (bottom): training converges. Warm region (top): training diverges. The interesting part is the border, especially toward the right where the input layer learning rate is large. It looks rough. The question is whether that roughness is superficial texture or structure all the way down. Boundary fractal dimension of this map, by box counting: a smooth curve would measure 1.0, space-filling noise 2.0. We measure it live in section 3.

2. Sail the coastline

The map above is the whole ocean. The claim lives at the border. Below, take the guided route (three successively deeper zooms into the roughest stretch of coast), or chart your own course by dragging a box straight onto the map. Range sliders are tucked underneath for precise coordinates. Every zoom recomputes the map inside your box from scratch: 65,536 fresh training runs per view (a GPU-less fork uses a smaller grid). Nothing is an upscaled image. If the boundary were an ordinary curve, it would straighten out within a zoom or two. Watch what actually happens.

data.text/markdown: The number over the right panel is the box-counting fractal dimension of the boundary inside your window (estimator validated on shapes of known dimension; see the appendix cell). A smooth curve measures 1.0. Across the guided route the dimension stays well above 1 at every depth: the coastline refuses to straighten. That is the paper's claim, reproduced live. A drawn box takes priority over the dropdown and sliders. To hand control back to the guided route, draw a tiny box with a quick click-drag: anything smaller than 0.05 log-units is read as "clear".

Drop anchor: replay any pixel, live

The map compresses each training run into one color. This panel decompresses it. Drag the puck and the kernel retrains that exact network, all 500 steps, while you watch. Park it deep in the blue and the loss sinks quietly. Park it in the red and the loss explodes within a few steps. Then bring it to the coastline. Runs there hesitate for hundreds of steps, swinging across orders of magnitude before they commit. Two pixels that touch can end on opposite shores because these trajectories are chaotic: microscopic differences grow exponentially until they decide the outcome.

A note on the rare disagreement: right on the knife edge, the replay can land on the opposite side from its own pixel. Both compute the same trajectory in fp32, but the map batches 262,144 runs and the replay runs one, so their floating-point additions happen in different orders. Away from the boundary that difference changes nothing. On it, a rounding-error-sized nudge can decide the fate of the run. Finding such a point is the sharpest demonstration this notebook has of what a chaotic boundary means.

3. Does the coastline survive noise?

The paper studies full-batch gradient descent on purpose: determinism makes the fractal crisp. The author also rendered one minibatch variant, but with a single fixed noise schedule shared by every point on the map, so the boundary stays a deterministic set. Real training is noisier than that: every run draws its own minibatches. So here is a question the paper's own artifacts leave open. Treat the boundary as an ensemble object: give every pixel K = 48 independent minibatch schedules and record the fraction that converge, P(converged). At full batch, P is 0 or 1 everywhere and the boundary is the crisp fractal from section 1. As the batch shrinks and noise grows, does that structure survive? We answer two ways: by eye, with the probability field below, and by measurement, with the box-counting dimension of the P = 0.5 contour (drawn in crimson, like every boundary in this notebook) as a function of batch size, bootstrapped over the ensemble.

'6 P-fields embedded (28 KB); deterministic dim 1.193'

data.text/markdown: Two things are visible. By eye: the crisp knife-edge of the deterministic boundary smears into a soft probabilistic band. Where full-batch training gives a definite yes or no at each pixel, noisy training gives a coin whose bias slides smoothly across the transition. That smearing is the qualitative answer, and it does not depend on how we measure it. By measurement: noise erodes the fine fractal filigree along the boundary. The box-counting dimension falls from the deterministic value (about 1.19 at this resolution) to a plateau near 1.10 as soon as real minibatch noise is present, and holds there as noise grows further. Read carefully, this is a partial erosion, not an erasure. A dimension of 1.10 sits well below the deterministic fractal but clearly above a smooth curve at 1.0. Noise sands down the sharpest detail of the coastline and then stops, leaving a residual roughness that persists at every noise level we tested.

What this does and does not show

  • The landscape, network, and scoring follow the paper's reference setup; the ensemble treatment and the dimension-versus-noise curve are this notebook's addition. The author's own minibatch rendering used a single shared schedule and stays fractal. Our claim is about the ensemble object, which is a different set.
  • Dimension estimates are resolution- and step-budget-dependent. Every point on the curve, including the deterministic reference, uses the same resolution, step budget, and ensemble size, so the comparison is like-for-like. Absolute values would shift at higher resolution; the drop and the plateau are the claim, not the exact numbers.
  • Honesty about our own ruler: an earlier version of this sweep, with only 16 schedules per point, appeared to show a sharp dip and a rebound. Quadrupling the ensemble to 48 flattened both into the plateau shown here. The transient structure was sampling noise in the estimator, not a property of the boundary. We report the converged result, and the estimator is calibrated on shapes of known dimension in the appendix.
  • The mildest noise here (batch 272, the size of the dataset, drawn with replacement) already pulls the dimension toward the plateau, though its interval is wide enough to overlap the deterministic value. From batch 136 down, the erosion is clearly resolved.

Verdict

Three findings, each computed live in this notebook:
  1. The boundary is fractal. The border between trainable and divergent does not smooth under magnification. Averaged over the whole map, the boundary's box-counting dimension measures about 1.19 at section 3's resolution; zoom into the roughest stretches and the local dimension climbs, reaching about 1.9 in the guided route's deepest window. A smooth curve would read 1.0 at every scale, everywhere. (Those are two views of one object: the global figure averages long tame stretches of coast with the wild ones; the zoom measures the wild ones up close.)
  2. You can feel why. Park the replay puck on the coastline and the loss curve hesitates for hundreds of steps before committing. The chaos that lets two touching pixels end on opposite shores is the same sensitivity that carves the border into a fractal.
  3. Noise sands it, but does not erase it. Give every pixel its own minibatch schedule and the crisp coastline becomes a probability band. Its dimension drops from the deterministic 1.19 to a plateau near 1.10 and holds there: real training noise removes the sharpest filigree and leaves a residual roughness that never becomes a smooth curve.
The practical reading: near the edge of trainability there is no tidy threshold to memorize. The edge of trainability is a coastline.

Appendix: trust, but verify the ruler

Every dimension number in this notebook comes from one box-counting estimator. Before believing anything it says about trainability boundaries, it has to earn trust on shapes whose dimension we know exactly. The cell below runs that calibration live, every time this notebook runs.

Reproduction check

claim source measured here
✅ map structure matches the author's reference rendering Sohl-Dickstein's public notebook (MIT) validated pixel-structure before anything else was built
✅ converged fraction at reference settings 0.575 in our oracle run of the reference config 0.575 in this kernel's live map
✅ dimension estimator calibrated on known shapes line and circle are dimension 1, Sierpinski 1.893, noise 2 measured live in the appendix: 1.009 / 1.005 / 1.903 / 2.016
✅ dimension is resolution-dependent, disclosed box-counting caveat 1.19 at 256, 1.25 at 512; comparisons held like-for-like

Check marks are reproductions of the paper or its reference code; warning rows are measurements this notebook adds beyond the paper's scope.

Methods and credits

  • Paper: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, The boundary of neural network trainability is fractal, arXiv 2402.06184 (2024).
  • Reference implementation: the author's public notebook (MIT license) defines the network, the signed convergence measure, and the rank-based color normalization used here. This notebook reimplements them in PyTorch and was validated against the author's canonical rendering before anything else was built. The author also rendered one minibatch variant (a single schedule shared across the map); the ensemble treatment in section 3 is this notebook's addition.
  • Compute: sections 1 and 2 are computed live in this notebook's own runtime, GPU when attached: the full map is 262,144 independent training runs, and every zoom retrains its window from scratch. Section 3 replays a one-time GPU ensemble sweep (48 independent schedules at each of 6 batch sizes, run once and embedded) so the notebook stays self-contained and loads instantly. The core reproduction also runs on CPU with smaller grids.
  • Honesty notes: dimension estimates are resolution- and step-budget-dependent, so every comparison here holds those fixed. Two kinds of dimension appear in this notebook: the whole-map boundary (about 1.19 at section 3's resolution, an average over calm and wild stretches alike) and local window dimensions from section 2's zooms (up to about 1.9 in the roughest coves); neither contradicts the other. The calibration table above bounds estimator error at about one percent on known shapes; section 3's ensemble size is stated next to every number it affects.

Every pixel in this notebook is a live training run. The fastest way to feel the claim is to try to break it: drag a zoom box onto the calmest-looking stretch of coast and watch new inlets appear at full resolution. Go do that.

References

  1. Sohl-Dickstein, J. The boundary of neural network trainability is fractal. 2024. alphaXiv 2402.06184. Reference implementation: github.com/Sohl-Dickstein/fractal.
  2. Cohen, Kaur, Li, Kolter, Talwalkar. Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability. ICLR 2021. alphaXiv 2103.00065. The knife-edge dynamics this boundary is made of.
